subject: Tenant Encapsulation & Egress Proofpoint — Q&A and Diagrams
messages:
From: David Lee <d.lee@fjordfinancial.com>
To: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Cc: Anna Schreiber <anna.schreiber@fjordfinancial.com>, security@fjordfinancial.com
Date: Tue, 3 Aug 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Tenant isolation diagrams + egress proofpoints (initial ask)

Kimberly,

Thanks for the quick turnaround on the RFP. Security has a couple of follow-ups before we can clear the next procurement milestone:

1) We need a concise diagram showing tenant encapsulation at the network and process level — specifically how a customer VPC, private deployment (VPC option), and hosted tenants are segmented across the control/data plane.
2) Please highlight egress paths and controls (bastions, NATs, sidecar proxies) and the expected externally routable endpoints. We need to know which public IPs (or ranges) we should allow.
3) A brief threat summary focused on cross-tenant data exfiltration vectors and mitigations is required for our internal security review.

Can you provide the diagram files, an allowlist matrix, and a short threat model summary today or early tomorrow? We have an internal security sync on Thursday.

Best,
David
Head of Cloud Security
Fjord Financial

From: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
To: David Lee <d.lee@fjordfinancial.com>
Cc: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai, marcus_lin@redwood.ai, irene_choi@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 3 Aug 2027 11:04:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant isolation diagrams + egress proofpoints (initial ask)

David —

Thanks for the clarity. I've attached three artifacts: a high-level deployment fabric diagram (redwood-deployment-fabric-v2.png), an IP/endpoint allowlist matrix (egress-allowlist-matrix.xlsx), and a concise threat-summary PDF (isolation-threat-summary-v1.pdf). Short answers inline below, and Marcus/Vanessa/Irène are looped for technical/controls detail.

- Encapsulation: We present three serving modalities in the diagram: Hosted (multi-tenant nodes with network-level tenant tagging and process-level sidecar isolation), Dedicated pools (customer-dedicated instances pinned to tenant-specific GPU pools), and Private (VPC-connected control plane with enforced subnet ACLs and private endpoints). The diagram annotates where mTLS and mutual attestation are enforced between control plane components and runtime nodes.

- Egress: Primary egress is via a customer-configurable egress gateway (sidecar + NAT) per deployment zone. For Private, traffic to customer backends stays on the VPC and egress is controlled by the customer's NAT/route tables. For Hosted, we publish a small set of CIDR ranges and fully-qualified hostnames that you can allow — see the first tab in the workbook.

- Mitigations vs cross-tenant exfil: Key controls are KV cache partitioning, strict RPC auth with short-lived tokens, namespace-scoped ephemeral storage, audit logging with immutable append-only traces, and runtime process isolation with cgroup-enforced limits + seccomp. The attached PDF lists threat scenarios and compensating controls.

We can clarify IP ranges and provide a per-region export if you want. Proposed next step: 30m call tomorrow morning to walk the diagram and answer any design questions.

Kimberly Park
Senior Product Security Manager, Redwood Inference

From: marcus_lin@redwood.ai
To: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, David Lee <d.lee@fjordfinancial.com>
Cc: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai, irene_choi@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 3 Aug 2027 13:28:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant isolation diagrams + egress proofpoints (technical addendum)

Adding a few technical clarifications to the artifacts Kimberly attached:

- Network demarcation: Each tenant is assigned a logical namespace within the mesh. For hosted mode we rely on VPP-based network namespaces on the node and per-tenant interface tagging. No tenant traffic traverses another tenant's namespace without explicit, logged brokering via the control plane.

- Sidecar behavior: Sidecars perform TLS termination for inbound model requests, enforce allowlists, and mediate outbound calls. They include an egress policy engine with workload-aware defaults to minimize broad 0.0.0.0/0 egress.

- KV cache: KV caches are sharded and keyed by tenant id. Cache eviction and purging are tenant-bound operations; cache reconciliation requires elevated ops privs and is auditable.

- Monitoring/audit: Trace IDs propagate from API to runtime and appear in audit artifacts. We retain token-level telemetry for 90 days (configurable under Dedicated/Private contracts).

Happy to join the walkthrough tomorrow to zoom into the diagram layers.

—Marcus
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Anna Schreiber <anna.schreiber@fjordfinancial.com>
To: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Cc: David Lee <d.lee@fjordfinancial.com>, security@fjordfinancial.com
Date: Wed, 4 Aug 2027 09:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant isolation diagrams + egress proofpoints (clarifications)

Thanks — the materials look promising. A couple of clarifying asks before the call:

1) For the hosted multi-tenant nodes, can you confirm whether inter-process access is blocked by default (deny-by-default) between tenant runtimes on the same host? We need explicit statement for our control gates.
2) Can you provide the per-region CIDR ranges you publish for hosted egress? The workbook lists aggregated ranges; we prefer the region split (us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1).

If you can confirm 1) in-line and provide 2) before the call, we'll be ready to sign off on the security checklist.

Regards,
Anna
Security Architect, Fjord Financial

From: vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai
To: Anna Schreiber <anna.schreiber@fjordfinancial.com>, David Lee <d.lee@fjordfinancial.com>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, marcus_lin@redwood.ai, irene_choi@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 4 Aug 2027 11:16:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Tenant isolation diagrams + egress proofpoints (confirmations + attachments)

Anna — quick answers and the region-split workbook attached.

1) Deny-by-default: Yes. Tenant runtimes are created in isolated network namespaces with kernel-level eBPF policies that default to deny for any cross-namespace connections. Only explicitly authorized control-plane channels or brokered service endpoints can be opened. That enforcement is baked into our node provisioning scripts and verified during image bake time.

2) Region CIDRs: See tab "region-cidrs" in the attached workbook (egress-allowlist-matrix.xlsx). We publish a minimal set of egress ranges per region; we also recommend using hostname-based allowlists where possible because some endpoints use dynamic host mapping behind our managed edge.

Also attached is a short checklist mapping each threat scenario to evidence artifacts (logs, attestation report ids). If anything in the walkthrough needs more depth, we can escalate to the runtime team for a focused session.

Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Product Security, Redwood Inference
